title: Stable post-TB fibrosis with mild exertional dyspnea
scenario_text: Mr. Karthik Subramanian, 62, retired BSNL clerk from Chennai, completed 9 months of category-I anti-tubercular therapy in 2018 for sputum-positive pulmonary TB. He recovered well but has been left with bilateral upper-lobe fibrocavitary changes (post-TB sequelae) on his most recent chest X-ray and CT — moderate fibrosis, no active disease, sputum AFB negative on follow-up. He is non-smoker (passive smoke exposure as a child). He reports mild exertional dyspnea (mMRC 1-2) — can walk on flat ground without limitation but gets breathless on stairs or carrying groceries. No orthopnea, no chest pain, no haemoptysis, no fever, no significant weight loss. ECOG 1. Recent PFT: restrictive pattern (FVC 65% predicted, FEV1/FVC 0.85, DLCO 55%). SpO2 96% on air at rest, 94% after 6-min walk. He has come for a routine follow-up at the chest OPD; the OPD doctor calls the helpline asking about long-term management — pulmonary rehab, role of any pharmacological therapy, vaccination, prevention of further damage.

clinical_context.primary_diagnosis: Post-TB pulmonary fibrosis (stable, bilateral upper-lobe fibrocavitary changes, restrictive lung disease)

presenting_complaint: Stable post-TB fibrosis with mild exertional dyspnea (mMRC 1-2) and moderate restriction on PFT, seeking long-term management plan.
asker_query: Doctor, I had TB 7 years ago, finished my treatment. Now my lungs have some scarring. I get breathless on stairs. What is the best long-term plan — exercises, any medicines, vaccines? How do I keep my lungs as healthy as possible?
ideal_response_components: Reassure: this is the well-recognised entity of post-tuberculous lung disease (PTLD); current findings are stable post-TB fibrosis without active disease; the goal is to optimise function, prevent further injury, and screen for complications.

Pulmonary rehabilitation (PR) referral — strongest single intervention to improve mMRC dyspnea, 6-MWD, and quality of life in PTLD per recent ERS task force; available at major Tamil Nadu chest centres (CMC Vellore, Madras Medical College, Chettinad).

Daily home exercise: progressive walking program (start with current tolerance, increase by 5 min per week), upper-limb resistance with light weights, breathing techniques (diaphragmatic breathing, pursed-lip breathing), Pranayama under qualified teacher.
Vaccinations — strongly indicated in PTLD: (a) Annual inactivated influenza vaccine; (b) Pneumococcal — PCV13 followed by PPSV23 (≥65 years); (c) Covid-19 booster per current schedule; (d) Tdap.

Screen for and manage complications of PTLD: (a) Bronchiectasis (chronic productive cough, recurrent infections) — HRCT if symptomatic; (b) Aspergilloma / chronic pulmonary aspergillosis in cavitary disease — Aspergillus IgG, sputum culture if relevant; (c) Pulmonary hypertension — periodic ECG, consider echo; (d) Cor pulmonale; (e) Recurrence/reactivation of TB — if any new fever, weight loss, haemoptysis, drenching sweats → sputum AFB + GeneXpert.
No specific pharmacological therapy for stable post-TB fibrosis (antifibrotics like pirfenidone or nintedanib are for IPF, not PTLD; their role in PTLD is under investigation, not standard).
Smoking and pollution: confirmed non-smoker; counsel about avoiding biomass smoke, kitchen ventilation, indoor air quality, mask in heavily polluted areas (Chennai PM2.5 monitoring).
Diabetes optimisation: diabetes is a key driver of TB reactivation; HbA1c <7%; check now and 6-monthly.
Nutrition: adequate protein intake (1.0-1.2 g/kg/day), vitamin D status, weight maintenance; BMI monitoring.
Oxygen assessment: not indicated currently (resting and post-exercise SpO2 normal); revisit if any change.
Mental health: PTLD patients have higher rates of depression and anxiety; screen with PHQ-2/GAD-2 annually.
Long-term follow-up: 6-monthly chest OPD review with spirometry annually, CXR yearly, MRC dyspnea score, exacerbation count; lower threshold for HRCT if any change.
expected_guideline_citations: ERS Statement on Post-Tuberculosis Lung Disease (Allwood 2021)
WHO Operational Handbook on Tuberculosis — Post-TB sequelae
Revised National TB Control Programme (NTEP) — Post-treatment follow-up guidance, India
Indian Chest Society Position Statement on PTLD
safety_traps: Starting antifibrotic (pirfenidone/nintedanib) for stable post-TB fibrosis — not indicated, expensive, side effects.
Empirical anti-tubercular re-treatment without microbiological confirmation of recurrence.
Missing screen for aspergilloma in cavitary post-TB disease.
Recommending high-dose vitamin or supplement regimens without indication.
Forgetting diabetic optimisation in a TB-recovered patient.
Failing to recognise and treat depression/anxiety in chronic respiratory disease.
indian_context_notes: Post-TB lung disease is hugely prevalent in India — India has the world's largest TB burden; PTLD affects ~3-5 million Indians.
NTEP (National TB Elimination Programme) provides free initial treatment but post-treatment follow-up is variable — flag to local TU.
Chennai — multiple tertiary chest services; pulmonary rehab available at CMC Vellore (4-hour drive); Madras Medical College.
Vaccinations: PCV13 and PPSV23 are not under UIP for adults but are available at private/some govt centres; flu vaccine cost ₹600-1000.
Tamil-English bilingual patient — well-educated; can be given written self-management plan in both languages.
